name: Social market economy
summary: The social market economy is the German postwar order of Erhard and Müller-Armack: a competitive market with free prices, independent control of monopolies and a strong state guarding the rules, joined to social security and stable money. It rejects both central planning and laissez-faire. Price stability, free trade and collective wage bargaining are central; the state shapes the framework but does not direct production.
scope: The model as set out by Ludwig Erhard, Alfred Müller-Armack and the CDU Düsseldorf Guidelines of 1949, 1948-1962. It excludes later EU usage of the phrase, and answers only what these texts state. Erhard and Müller-Armack differ on the scope of social compensation and on European institutions.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Guideline 4 demands a central body to protect the currency, and Erhard works with the central bank on currency stability.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The model rests on market prices, money and performance-based pay set by collective agreement.

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: The model rests on wages fixed by collective agreement and performance-based pay.

all-land-state-owned.rationale: Principle 10 affirms private property and aims to make the poorer classes owners, which excludes state or community ownership of all land.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Erhard lists deficit spending among dogmas and says a state refusing to sin against the currency can spend only what it has taxed, though Guideline 13 backs public investment against crises.

ban-cartels.rationale: Principle 1 requires an independent authority controlling monopolies, and Erhard (ch. VII) defends the principle of prohibiting cartels.

capital-controls.rationale: Erhard lists as achievements the loosening of limits on payments, capital movement and investment abroad and demands free convertibility.

central-planning.rationale: The Guidelines state that the command economy is rejected whether its guiding agencies are central or decentralized, state or autonomous.

class-collaboration.rationale: Guideline 16 makes the model depend on entrepreneurs, workers and consumers taking part, and Müller-Armack calls it an integration formula leading social forces to cooperation.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Principle 7 says wages and working conditions must be left to the collective agreement system.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Principle 10 affirms private property as the basis of the economy, which excludes holding the means of production in common by community.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: The Guidelines reject guidance of the economy by any agency, state or autonomous, and leave only wage fixing to collective agreements; bodies setting wages and prices together are ruled out.

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: Erhard attacks the Welfare State as dependency but says he does not wish to change existing social security and sees room to extend it.

economic-freedom.rationale: Erhard presents the market economy as the rejection of tyranny and totalitarianism, a middle way between unbridled liberalism and totalitarianism.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Erhard and the Guidelines call for a free world market and convertible currencies, which a closed self-sufficient bloc contradicts.

free-trade.rationale: Erhard argued liberalization is right in principle even without reciprocity, and the Guidelines aim to promote foreign trade by all possible means.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Principle 10 affirms private property and aims to make the poorer classes owners, which excludes state or community ownership of all land.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The Guidelines say market-driven prices regulate the interaction of all participants and reject the command economy, and Erhard builds his whole programme on competition and free prices.

municipal-property.rationale: Principle 10 affirms private property as the basis of the economy, which excludes holding the means of production in common by community.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Erhard says a modern and responsible state cannot return to the night-watchman role, and the scholarship stresses a strong state guaranteeing the order.

no-business-privileges.rationale: The ordoliberal state in this model is strong enough to resist privilege-seeking interest groups, and Erhard opposes special interests in his ministry.

no-central-bank.rationale: Guideline 4 demands a central body to protect the currency, and Erhard works with the central bank on currency stability.

one-party-rule.rationale: Erhard rejects intolerance leading to tyranny and totalitarianism, and the Guidelines aim to secure political democracy.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Müller-Armack names European integration one of two guiding models, while Erhard rejects transferring sectors to supranational authorities; the strands differ.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: The Guidelines say prices must not be distorted by state decree, and Erhard lifted price controls in 1948 despite scarcity and opposed an independent price bureau.

price-controls-fight-inflation.rationale: Erhard held that suppressed inflation paralyses the economy and fought inflation through currency and credit policy and free prices, not price controls.

price-stability-first.rationale: Erhard says the price level must in all circumstances be maintained and that social policy not treating currency stability as of first importance endangers the model.

property-fundamental.rationale: Principle 10 affirms and promotes private property, though it also admits public ownership where useful, so it is not an absolute right.

public-ownership.rationale: Private property is the default, and public ownership is allowed only where economically useful, feasible and politically necessary (principle 10).

regulate-corporations.rationale: The Guidelines call for stricter reporting duties for incorporated firms, legal measures fostering business responsibility and independent control of economic power.

social-market-economy.rationale: The Düsseldorf Guidelines define the social market economy as performance-based competition with independent monopoly control and a social policy, set against both the command economy and liberal free enterprise.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The Guidelines refrain from planning and guiding production, labour or sales, allowing only market-conforming policy; directing investment to chosen industries is such guidance.

state-harmful.rationale: The model rests on a strong state that sets and guards the competitive order, so a state that is unnecessary and harmful contradicts it.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Erhard limits compulsory state insurance to the needy, and Müller-Armack wants social assistance concentrated on those who really need it.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Erhard cut tariffs from 1955 to bring competition in from abroad and held protectionist walls foster monopolies; the Guidelines promote foreign trade by all means.

taxation-theft.rationale: The model funds an active state and social policy from taxation, and the Guidelines call for tax reform and cuts, not abolition.

total-state.rationale: The Guidelines reject the command economy and Erhard rejects totalitarianism, so a state directing every area of life contradicts them.

unions-run-economy.rationale: The Guidelines reject economic guidance by autonomous bodies as much as by the state and confine unions to collective wage agreements.

notes: Most statements outside economic order, trade and money are null: the sources do not address them. Themes searched: economy, world, government, liberty, ecology, technology, society.
